props.title: White Man's Burden
props.initialSlug: Role reversal drama in a racially flipped America

sections.content: White Man's Burden represents a bold but flawed attempt at racial role reversal in American cinema. John Travolta and Harry Belafonte star in this alternate reality where Black Americans are the dominant social group and whites face systemic discrimination. While its execution received mixed reviews, the film belongs in conversation with other 90s racial discourse films like Higher Learning (1995) and Dangerous Minds (1995), though it takes a more experimental approach than either. The film's premise draws conceptual parallels to the groundbreaking Nothing But a Man (1964), though inverting the power dynamics.

sections.content: The film's greatest strength lies in its premise rather than its execution. Director Desmond Nakano attempts what Get Out (2017) would later achieve more successfully - using genre elements to explore racial dynamics in America. The role reversal concept recalls elements of Watermelon Man (1970), Melvin Van Peebles' satire about a white bigot who wakes up Black. Both films use high-concept premises to examine privilege and prejudice, though White Man's Burden takes a more dramatic approach.

The film's release in 1995 came during a period of heightened mainstream discourse around race relations, following the LA Riots and O.J. Simpson trial. Similar themes emerged in films like Devil in a Blue Dress (1995) and Clockers (1995), though those works approached racial issues through more conventional narrative structures. White Man's Burden's alternate reality concept predates later works like Sorry to Bother You (2018) that would use surreal elements to discuss race and class. SUBHEAD: Impact and Legacy

movies.slug: Jordan Peele's groundbreaking horror film about a young Black man uncovering disturbing secrets while meeting his white girlfriend's family

sections.content: While not commercially successful, White Man's Burden helped pave the way for more experimental examinations of race in American cinema. Films like Dear White People (2014) and BlacKkKlansman (2018) would later blend genres and tones to address similar themes with greater critical acclaim. The film's premise remains relevant to discussions of perspective and privilege, even as its execution shows its age.
